questions.q: AIDS was first recognised as a new disease in the year:
questions.x: AIDS was first described in the USA in 1981; HIV was identified as its cause shortly afterwards.

questions.q: Poliovirus enters the body through the mouth and causes paralysis by destroying:
o: Red blood cells in the liver
Cells lining the air sacs of the lungs
Motor neurons in the spinal cord
questions.x: Poliovirus spreads by the faecal–oral route and can invade the nervous system, killing motor neurons of the spinal cord so that muscles become paralysed.

questions.q: Ammonia released by deamination must be quickly converted into urea in mammals because ammonia is:
questions.x: Ammonia is very toxic even in low concentration, so the liver converts it into much less toxic urea, which is then excreted by the kidneys.

questions.q: An ATP molecule is made of:
o: Adenine, deoxyribose and three phosphate groups
Adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups
Adenine, glucose and two phosphate groups
Guanine, ribose and three phosphate groups
questions.x: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) contains the base adenine, the five-carbon sugar ribose and a chain of three phosphate groups. Deoxyribose is the sugar of DNA, not ATP.

questions.q: A decarboxylation reaction in respiration is one that:
o: Adds carbon dioxide to a molecule
Adds a phosphate group to a molecule
Removes carbon dioxide from a molecule
questions.x: Decarboxylation removes a carboxyl carbon as carbon dioxide, as in the link reaction and two steps of the Krebs cycle. Removing hydrogen is dehydrogenation.

questions.q: Which substance dissolves in water by forming hydrogen bonds with water molecules, rather than by separating into ions?
questions.x: Glucose has many polar –OH groups that hydrogen-bond with water. Sodium chloride and magnesium sulphate dissolve by splitting into ions, and cooking oil is non-polar and does not dissolve.

questions.q: The main storage carbohydrate in potato tubers and cereal grains is:
questions.x: Plants store surplus glucose as starch in tubers and grains. Cellulose is structural, glycogen is the animal store, and sucrose is the transported sugar.

questions.q: A polypeptide chain has two different ends. The end that has a free amino group is called the:
questions.x: The amino acid at the start of the chain has a free –NH₂ (the N-terminus); the last has a free –COOH (the C-terminus). All other amino and carboxyl groups are used in peptide bonds.

questions.q: The covalent bond that joins one monosaccharide to another is called a:
questions.x: Monosaccharides are linked through an oxygen bridge called a glycosidic bond. Peptide bonds join amino acids, ester bonds join fatty acids to glycerol, and hydrogen bonds are weak attractions, not covalent links.

questions.q: How does a membrane glycolipid differ from a membrane glycoprotein?
o: A glycolipid has sugar chains, but a glycoprotein has none
A glycolipid faces the cytoplasm, but a glycoprotein faces outside
In a glycolipid the sugar chain is attached to a lipid; in a glycoprotein it is attached to a protein
A glycolipid contains amino acids, but a glycoprotein contains none
questions.x: Both carry carbohydrate chains on the outer surface. They differ in what the sugar is attached to: a lipid in glycolipids and a protein in glycoproteins.

questions.q: In a sucrose molecule, glucose and fructose are joined by a glycosidic bond between:
o: Carbon 1 of glucose and carbon 4 of fructose
Carbon 1 of glucose and carbon 6 of fructose
Carbon 1 of glucose and carbon 2 of fructose
Carbon 4 of glucose and carbon 4 of fructose
questions.x: Sucrose has an α(1→2) linkage that joins the reducing carbons of both sugars (C-1 of glucose, C-2 of fructose). This is why sucrose is a non-reducing sugar.

questions.q: One complete turn of the DNA double helix contains about 10 base pairs. Each base pair is therefore rotated relative to the next by about:
questions.x: A full turn is 360°, shared among about 10 base pairs, so each step turns about 360° ÷ 10 = 36°. The figure 0.34 nm is the rise per base pair, not an angle.

questions.q: A trisaccharide is made of three hexose units, each C6H12O6 with a molecular mass of 180. Water has a mass of 18. What is the molecular mass of the trisaccharide?
questions.x: Three hexoses join by two glycosidic bonds, releasing two water molecules. Mass = 3 × 180 − 2 × 18 = 540 − 36 = 504.

questions.q: DNA controls the characteristics of a cell mainly by:
o: Supplying energy for all cell reactions
Directing the synthesis of specific proteins, including enzymes
Forming the outer membrane of the cell
questions.x: Genes in DNA code for proteins, and these proteins (many of them enzymes) decide the cell's structure and chemistry. DNA does not supply energy, form membranes or store glucose.

questions.q: The base pairing in the Watson–Crick model at once suggested how DNA could be copied, because:
o: Each strand can serve as a template for a new complementary strand
The bases lie outside the helix where enzymes can reach them
The two strands are identical in base sequence
The helix contains exactly ten base pairs per turn
questions.x: Because A pairs only with T and G only with C, each strand fixes the sequence of its partner, so each can act as a template. The two strands are complementary, not identical.

questions.q: Which pair of nucleotide-based molecules act as coenzymes that carry hydrogen in respiration and photosynthesis?
questions.x: NAD and NADP are dinucleotide coenzymes that accept and pass on hydrogen in redox reactions. The other pairs are sugars, structural proteins and storage polysaccharides.

questions.q: In many bacteria, infoldings of the plasma membrane that are thought to help in respiration and DNA replication are called:
questions.x: Mesosomes are inward folds of the bacterial plasma membrane. Cristae are folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane, which bacteria do not have.

questions.q: Besides cellulose, the primary cell wall of a plant cell contains:
questions.x: The primary wall has cellulose microfibrils set in a matrix of hemicellulose and pectin. Chitin is found in fungal walls and peptidoglycan in bacterial walls.

questions.q: In a mature plant cell, the nucleus usually lies near the cell wall rather than in the centre because:
o: The large central vacuole pushes the cytoplasm and nucleus to the edge
The cell wall attracts the nucleus
Plant cells have no cytoplasm in the centre of young cells
Centrioles pull the nucleus to one side
questions.x: The big central vacuole takes up most of the volume of a mature plant cell, pressing the cytoplasm and nucleus against the wall. In animal cells the nucleus is usually central.

questions.q: A small knob at the end of a chromosome, separated from the rest of the arm by a secondary constriction, is called a:
questions.x: Chromosomes with a satellite are called SAT chromosomes; the satellite is joined to the arm across a secondary constriction. The centromere is the primary constriction.

questions.q: Most of the DNA of a eukaryotic cell is found in the:
questions.x: Nearly all the cell's DNA is in the chromosomes of the nucleus; mitochondria carry only a small circular DNA, and the Golgi and ribosomes have none.

questions.q: Baroreceptors in the walls of major arteries respond directly to changes in:
questions.x: Baroreceptors are stretch-sensitive mechanoreceptors; a change in blood pressure changes how much the artery wall is stretched. Oxygen level is sensed by chemoreceptors.

questions.q: Which of the following is a lobe of each cerebral hemisphere?
questions.x: Each cerebral hemisphere has frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes. The pons is part of the brainstem, the vermis joins the cerebellar hemispheres, and the thalamus lies deep in the forebrain.

questions.q: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus are stimulated mainly by a change in the:
o: Solute concentration (osmotic pressure) of the blood
Stretch of the urinary bladder wall
questions.x: Osmoreceptors detect changes in the osmotic pressure (water and solute balance) of the blood. Bladder stretch is detected by mechanoreceptors.

questions.q: A cross-section of part of the central nervous system shows white matter on the outside and an H-shaped area of grey matter around a narrow central canal. The section is from the:
questions.x: In the spinal cord grey matter is central and H-shaped, with white matter around it. In the cerebrum and cerebellum the arrangement is the reverse: an outer grey cortex over inner white matter.

questions.q: In the skin, a thermoreceptor acts as a transducer that converts:
questions.x: A thermoreceptor detects heat (temperature change) and converts it into nerve impulses. Receptors always produce impulses as their output, not the other way round.

questions.q: Unlike an action potential, the generator (receptor) potential produced in a receptor:
o: Is always of exactly the same size
Travels along the whole axon without change
Is produced only by stimuli above threshold
Varies in size with the strength of the stimulus
questions.x: A generator potential is graded: a stronger stimulus gives a larger one. Only when it reaches threshold does it set up all-or-none action potentials in the sensory neuron.

questions.q: Bipolar neurons, with one dendrite and one axon on opposite sides of the cell body, are found in the:
o: Ventral horn of the spinal cord
questions.x: Bipolar neurons occur in the retina (and in the olfactory epithelium). Ventral horn and motor cortex neurons are multipolar, and dorsal root ganglia hold unipolar sensory neurons.

questions.q: The enzyme acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic cleft breaks acetylcholine down into:
questions.x: Acetylcholinesterase hydrolyses acetylcholine to choline and acetate, ending its action. The choline is taken back into the knob and reused.

questions.q: Seeds sown in very cold soil germinate slowly mainly because:
o: Their enzymes are denatured by the cold
Their starch is converted into protein
Their enzymes work very slowly at low temperature
questions.x: Low temperature reduces the kinetic energy of molecules, so enzyme reactions such as starch digestion in the seed are slow. The enzymes are not denatured.

questions.q: A deficiency of certain B-group vitamins slows many metabolic reactions. The reason is that:
o: Coenzymes are made from these vitamins, so the enzymes that need them cannot work
These vitamins are the substrates of those reactions
questions.x: Many coenzymes, such as NAD⁺ and FAD, are built from B-group vitamins. Without the coenzyme, the apoenzyme is inactive.

questions.q: In a metabolic pathway A → B → C → D:
o: One enzyme catalyses all the steps
Enzymes are needed only for the first step
The end product D acts as the enzyme for every step
Each step is catalysed by its own specific enzyme
questions.x: Because enzymes are specific, each step of a pathway generally needs a different enzyme.

questions.q: In feedback inhibition, the end product usually inhibits the first enzyme of the pathway rather than the last one because:
o: The last enzyme has no active site
This stops the whole pathway early, so raw materials and intermediates are not wasted
Inhibition of the first enzyme is always irreversible
The end product has the same shape as the first substrate
questions.x: Blocking the first step prevents intermediates from piling up and saves the starting material for other uses.

questions.q: The variety of Galápagos finches, each with a beak suited to a different food, all arising from one ancestral species, is an example of:
questions.x: Adaptive radiation is the evolution of many species from one ancestor, each suited to a different way of life. The finches are the classic example.

questions.q: In 1858, the theory of natural selection was first presented publicly in a joint paper by Darwin and Wallace to the:
questions.x: Papers by Darwin and Wallace were read together at the Linnean Society of London in 1858, a year before On the Origin of Species was published.

questions.q: Miller identified the organic products formed in his apparatus by using:
questions.x: Miller analysed the solution with paper chromatography and detected several amino acids. Culturing would detect living organisms, which the sterile apparatus did not contain.

questions.q: In a vasectomy, a small part of each vas deferens is cut and tied. Which result is expected?
o: Semen contains no sperm, but testosterone secretion continues normally
Testosterone secretion stops, so male features are lost
No semen at all is produced
Sperm production in the testes stops completely
questions.x: Cutting the vas deferens blocks the passage of sperm, so the ejaculate lacks sperm. The Leydig cells and the glands that make seminal fluid are not affected.

questions.q: After childbirth, the production of milk by the mammary glands is stimulated mainly by:
questions.x: Prolactin from the anterior pituitary stimulates milk production. Oxytocin causes the milk to be ejected (let down) during suckling.

questions.q: A person infected with HIV two weeks ago gives a negative result on an HIV antibody test. The most likely reason is that:
o: HIV is destroyed within two weeks
HIV is never found in blood
Antibodies against HIV have not yet been made in detectable amounts
questions.x: It takes some weeks for the body to make enough antibodies to be detected; this gap is the window period. During it, the person can still pass on the virus.

questions.q: Erection of the penis occurs when:
o: Its spongy erectile tissue fills with blood
Its muscles contract around a bone
The testes rise into the abdomen
questions.x: The penis contains spongy erectile tissue. When its arteries dilate, blood fills these spaces and the penis becomes firm. Humans have no bone in the penis.

questions.q: A whole skeletal muscle such as the biceps is made of bundles of muscle fibres. Each bundle is wrapped in:
questions.x: Skeletal muscle fibres are grouped into bundles held together and wrapped by connective tissue, which also carries blood vessels and nerves and continues into the tendons.

questions.q: In a thin filament of skeletal muscle, the long thread-like tropomyosin molecules lie:
o: Along the grooves of the twisted actin chains
Inside the hollow core of the thick filament
Across the Z line, joining two sarcomeres
Within the membrane of the sarcoplasmic reticulum
questions.x: Tropomyosin is a long fibrous protein that lies in the grooves of the actin double helix. In this position it can cover the myosin-binding sites on actin.

questions.q: Astronauts who spend months in weightlessness lose bone mass. The best explanation is that, without weight-bearing:
o: Osteoblasts become more active than osteoclasts
Bone marrow is converted into cartilage
Collagen in bone is replaced by elastic fibres
questions.x: Bone is remodelled according to the loads it bears. With no weight on the skeleton, osteoclasts remove more bone than osteoblasts lay down, so bone density falls.

questions.q: As a skeletal muscle fibre contracts, the region where thick and thin filaments overlap:
questions.x: Thin filaments slide further in between the thick filaments, so the overlap region grows while the I band and H zone shrink. It is the H zone, not the overlap, that can disappear.

questions.q: Which pair contains only joints that allow movement around a single axis?
questions.x: A hinge bends in one plane and a pivot rotates around one axis, so both are single-axis joints. Saddle and condyloid joints move in two planes, and ball-and-socket joints in all planes.

questions.q: The pattern of gout over time is typically:
o: Slow, steady worsening over decades with no flares
Constant mild pain from childhood onward
A single attack that never returns
Sudden painful attacks separated by periods with no symptoms
questions.x: Gout usually comes as sudden flares lasting days, with symptom-free gaps between attacks. Slow, steady worsening over many years is the pattern of osteoarthritis.

questions.q: The ribs that are joined directly to the sternum by their own costal cartilages are the:
questions.x: The first seven pairs are true ribs, each with its own costal cartilage to the sternum. Pairs 8–10 join through the cartilage above, and pairs 11–12 are floating ribs with no front attachment.

questions.q: The tiny arrector pili muscles that make the hairs of the skin stand up are made of:
questions.x: Arrector pili muscles are small bundles of involuntary smooth muscle attached to hair follicles. We cannot raise our hairs at will.

questions.q: A red-eyed female Drosophila crossed with a red-eyed male gives 120 offspring, of which 30 are white-eyed males. Which conclusion is correct?
o: The female is heterozygous, and no white-eyed females are expected
The female is homozygous red, and some white-eyed females are expected
The male carries the white allele on his Y
Both parents are heterozygous, so a quarter of the females are white-eyed
questions.x: White-eyed sons must get Xʷ from the mother, so she is XᵂXʷ. Every daughter gets the father's red X, so none are white-eyed.

questions.q: A recombination frequency of 0% between two genes shows that they are:
o: Separated by crossing over in every meiosis
questions.x: No recombinants means crossing over never separated the genes, which is complete linkage. Unlinked genes or genes on different chromosomes give 50% recombination.

questions.q: A plant has the repulsion arrangement Ab/aB of two genes that never cross over, with complete dominance. On selfing, its progeny phenotypes appear in the ratio:
questions.x: Only Ab and aB gametes form, giving Ab/Ab, Ab/aB and aB/aB in a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio. These show the phenotypes A_bb, A_B_ and aaB_; no aabb appears.

questions.q: Crossing over alters which of the following?
o: The combination of alleles carried on a chromatid
The number of chromosomes in each gamete
questions.x: Crossing over swaps corresponding segments between homologues, so it reshuffles alleles on chromatids. The number of chromosomes and the ploidy are unchanged.

questions.q: Crossing over does not normally occur in male Drosophila. A grey long male (BV/bv) is crossed with a black vestigial female. The offspring will be:
o: Mostly parental types with a few recombinants
Grey long and black vestigial only, 1 : 1
questions.x: Without crossing over, the male forms only BV and bv gametes, so only the two parental phenotypes appear in equal numbers. This is complete linkage.

questions.q: Hairy ear rims are inherited as a holandric trait. Which grandchildren of an affected man will certainly inherit it from him?
o: All the sons of his daughters
All the children of his daughters
All the sons of his sons
All the daughters of his sons
questions.x: A Y-linked gene passes from father to every son, and then on to every son of those sons. Daughters receive no Y, so the trait cannot pass through them.

questions.q: A woman who is a carrier for hemophilia usually has normal blood clotting because:
o: Her Y chromosome carries a normal allele
Her one normal allele makes enough of the clotting factor
The hemophilia allele is not expressed in females
questions.x: A carrier is XᴴXʰ. The normal allele on one X produces enough clotting factor, so the recessive allele is masked.

questions.q: Which cells of a normal human male contain an X chromosome but no Y chromosome?
questions.x: Body cells and primary spermatocytes are XY. When the sex chromosomes separate in meiosis, half the sperm receive the X and half the Y.

questions.q: Cancer cells from a tumour in the breast often reach the lymph nodes of the armpit first. This is because:
o: Armpit nodes produce the cancer cells
Arteries carry cancer cells directly into the armpit
Lymph from the breast drains through the armpit nodes
The thoracic duct begins in the armpit
questions.x: Lymph from the breast passes through the armpit (axillary) nodes, so cells that escape into lymph are often trapped there first.

questions.q: The pointed lower tip of the heart, formed mainly by the left ventricle, is called the:
questions.x: The cone-shaped heart has a broad base above, where the great vessels attach, and a pointed apex below, formed by the left ventricle.

questions.q: An artificial pacemaker is fitted in a patient whose:
o: Coronary arteries are narrowed by fat
Heart's own impulse-generating or conducting system does not work properly
questions.x: An artificial pacemaker sends regular electrical impulses to the heart muscle when the natural pacemaker or conduction pathway fails. Leaky valves and blocked arteries need other treatment.

questions.q: Lymph enters a lymph node and leaves it through vessels called, respectively, the:
questions.x: Several afferent vessels bring lymph into a node and fewer efferent vessels carry the filtered lymph out.

questions.q: Antigen recognition depends on receptor molecules on the cell surface. Such receptors are present on:
questions.x: Both kinds of lymphocyte have surface receptors for a specific antigen: B-cell receptors are membrane antibodies, and T cells have T-cell receptors.

questions.q: Humoral immunity is mainly effective against:
o: Viruses that are hidden inside body cells
Bacteria and toxins circulating in the body fluids
questions.x: Antibodies act in plasma and lymph, so they deal best with free bacteria, viruses outside cells and toxins. Infected cells, cancer cells and grafts are mainly handled by T cells.

questions.q: Plasma cells are packed with rough endoplasmic reticulum because they:
o: Make and secrete large amounts of antibody protein
questions.x: Antibodies are proteins made on ribosomes of the rough ER, and a plasma cell secretes thousands of them per second, so it needs a very large amount of rough ER.

questions.q: Impulses from the respiratory centre reach the diaphragm through the:
questions.x: The phrenic nerves carry motor impulses to the diaphragm, making it contract during inspiration. The vagus nerves mainly carry sensory information from the lungs back to the brain.

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches a component of tobacco smoke with its main harmful effect?
o: Tar: makes the heart beat faster
Carbon monoxide: reduces the oxygen carried by the blood
questions.x: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin and lowers oxygen transport. Nicotine is the addictive stimulant that speeds the heart, and tar carries most of the carcinogens.

questions.q: Smoke rising from the burning tip of a cigarette (sidestream smoke) is harmful to people nearby because:
o: It contains no carbon monoxide but much more oxygen
It is not filtered and contains high levels of harmful substances
It is breathed only by the smoker
Its particles are too large to enter the lungs
questions.x: Sidestream smoke goes directly into the air without passing through the cigarette or the smoker's lungs, so it carries high concentrations of tar, carbon monoxide and other toxins that bystanders inhale.

questions.q: The final digestion of peptides into amino acids in the small intestine is carried out by:
questions.x: Peptidases, together called erepsin, in the intestinal juice and on the epithelial cells finish protein digestion to amino acids. Pepsin only makes polypeptides, bile has no enzymes, and lipase acts on fats.

questions.q: Dental caries (tooth decay) begins when:
o: Fluoride in water softens the dentine
The pulp cavity fills with cementum
Bacteria in plaque ferment sugars into acids that dissolve the enamel
questions.x: Plaque bacteria feed on sugars left on the teeth and produce acids, which dissolve the enamel and then the dentine. Fluoride actually makes enamel more resistant to acid.

questions.q: If blood passed through the peritubular network before reaching the glomerulus, what would most directly go wrong?
o: The tubule cells would receive no blood
Glomerular pressure would be too low for effective filtration
The urine would contain red blood cells
questions.x: Blood loses pressure as it crosses a capillary bed. Coming straight from the afferent arteriole is what keeps glomerular pressure high; after a capillary network it would be too low to filter well.

questions.q: A drug bound to plasma proteins is hardly filtered at the glomerulus, yet it can still be excreted quickly in urine because it is:
o: Secreted from peritubular blood into the tubule
Converted into urea in the PCT
questions.x: What escapes filtration can still be removed by tubular secretion: the tubule cells take the drug from peritubular blood and pass it into the tubule fluid.

questions.q: Laser treatment of a kidney stone works by:
o: Breaking the stone into small fragments with focused light energy
Dissolving the stone with strong acid
Freezing the stone so that it shrinks
Drawing the stone out through the skin
questions.x: A laser fibre brought up to the stone delivers intense light energy that shatters it, and the fragments pass out or are removed.

questions.q: Going from the outside of a kidney inwards, which order of regions is met?
o: Cortex → renal capsule → medulla → renal pelvis
Renal capsule → medulla → cortex → renal pelvis
Renal capsule → renal pelvis → cortex → medulla
Renal capsule → cortex → medulla → renal pelvis
questions.x: The fibrous capsule covers the outer cortex. Inside lies the medulla with its pyramids, which drain into the renal pelvis near the hilum.

questions.q: Cells of the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle contain many mitochondria. This suits them for:
o: Filtering plasma out of the blood
Secreting plasma proteins into the filtrate
Actively pumping sodium and chloride ions out of the filtrate
questions.x: The ascending limb pumps out salts by active transport, which needs much ATP from mitochondria. It is impermeable to water, and filtration happens only at the glomerulus.

questions.q: Which is the correct order of steps in shock-wave lithotripsy?
o: Waves focused on stone, stone located, fragments pass in urine, stone breaks up
Stone located by imaging, waves focused on it, stone breaks up, fragments pass in urine
Fragments pass in urine, stone located, waves focused, stone breaks up
Stone breaks up, stone located, waves focused, fragments pass in urine
questions.x: The stone must first be located so the waves can be aimed at it; only after it breaks can the small pieces be passed in the urine.

questions.q: Water reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule is called 'obligatory' because it:
o: Takes place only when the person is dehydrated
Requires ATP to pump water molecules
Always follows the reabsorbed solutes, whatever the body's water needs
questions.x: In the PCT water moves by osmosis after the solutes, whether or not the body is short of water. ADH-controlled water uptake happens later, in the DCT and collecting duct.

questions.q: A person with normal fluid intake starts passing very little urine each day. This suggests:
questions.x: A sharp fall in urine output (oliguria) is a typical sign that the kidneys are failing. Diabetes insipidus causes large volumes of dilute urine.

questions.q: Taking very large doses of vitamin D for a long time can lead to kidney stones because it:
o: Increases calcium absorption from the gut, so more calcium reaches the urine
Stops the liver from making urea
Lowers the water content of the urine directly
questions.x: Vitamin D promotes calcium absorption. Too much raises blood and urine calcium, favouring calcium stones.

questions.q: In humans, urea leaves the body mainly in:
questions.x: Urea is carried in the plasma to the kidneys and excreted in urine. Only small amounts are lost in sweat.

questions.q: The tetanus and diphtheria vaccines contain toxoids. A toxoid is:
o: A bacterial toxin made harmless by treatment but still able to stimulate antibody production
A live bacterium with its toxin gene removed
An antibody made against the toxin in a horse
A synthetic antibiotic that destroys the toxin
questions.x: Toxoids are toxins inactivated, for example with formaldehyde, so they no longer cause harm but keep their antigenic shape. The body makes antibodies (antitoxins) and memory cells against them.

questions.q: tPA is helpful in a stroke caused by a blood clot but would be dangerous in a stroke caused by bleeding in the brain. The reason is that tPA:
o: Raises the blood glucose level sharply
Breaks down fibrin, so it would prevent bleeding from being stopped by clotting
questions.x: tPA activates plasmin, which digests the fibrin of clots. In a bleeding stroke, clots are needed to seal the damaged vessel, so dissolving them would make the bleeding worse.

questions.q: During gel electrophoresis of DNA fragments, the smallest fragments:
o: Move farthest towards the positive electrode
questions.x: DNA is negatively charged because of its phosphate groups, so it moves towards the positive electrode. Small fragments slip through the gel more easily and travel farthest.

questions.q: A preparation has a theoretical yield of 25 g and a percentage yield of 60%. What mass of product is actually obtained?
questions.x: Actual yield = 60/100 × 25 = 15 g. 10 g is the mass lost, and 41.7 g comes from dividing 25 by 0.6.

questions.q: Iron and sulphur are heated together: Fe + S → FeS. A mixture contains 5.6 g of iron and 4.0 g of sulphur. Which is the limiting reactant? (Fe = 56, S = 32)
o: Sulphur, because its mass is smaller
Sulphur, because 0.125 mol S is less than 0.1 mol Fe
Iron, because 0.1 mol Fe is less than 0.125 mol S
Neither, because they react in a 1 : 1 mass ratio
questions.x: Fe = 5.6/56 = 0.1 mol; S = 4.0/32 = 0.125 mol. With a 1 : 1 mole ratio, iron runs out first and 0.025 mol S is left. A smaller mass does not mean fewer moles.

questions.q: In the ground state of carbon (Z = 6), the two 2p electrons are:
o: In different 2p orbitals with parallel spins
In different 2p orbitals with opposite spins
questions.x: By Hund's rule, electrons enter degenerate 2p orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing, so carbon has two unpaired electrons.

questions.q: Hydrogen atoms are excited so that their electrons reach n = 4. As they return to the ground state, the maximum number of different spectral lines possible is:
Which statement correctly relates principal energy levels, sub-levels and orbitals?
o: A principal energy level contains sub-levels, and each sub-level contains one or more orbitals
An orbital contains several sub-levels, each with its own energy
A sub-level contains several principal energy levels
Each principal energy level contains exactly one orbital
questions.x: The hierarchy is shell (n) → sub-levels (s, p, d, f) → orbitals (1, 3, 5, 7). For example, n = 2 has 2s and 2p, and 2p has three orbitals.

questions.q: In the van der Waals equation, both correction terms, an²/V² and nb, become negligible when the gas:
o: Is highly compressed at low temperature
Is cooled close to its boiling point
Occupies a very large volume, at low pressure
questions.x: In a very large volume, an²/V² is tiny and nb is small compared with V, so the equation reduces to PV = nRT. This is why real gases are nearly ideal at low pressure.

questions.q: Using SI values for 1 mol of an ideal gas, P = 101325 N m⁻², V = 0.022414 m³ and T = 273.15 K, the value of R obtained is:
questions.x: R = (101325 × 0.022414)/(1 × 273.15) ≈ 8.314 N m K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. This is the SI value, because SI units of pressure and volume were used.

questions.q: Gas X is at 0 °C and gas Y is at 273 °C. Compared with the molecules of X, the molecules of Y have an average kinetic energy that is:
questions.x: Kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature: 273 K for X and 546 K for Y, a ratio of 1 : 2. The Celsius values cannot be used for this ratio.

questions.q: A hydrogen bond is best described as:
o: A covalent bond shared between two molecules
An ionic bond between H⁺ and an anion
questions.x: The partly positive H on F, O or N is attracted electrostatically to a lone pair on a neighbouring electronegative atom; it is a strong kind of dipole–dipole force.

questions.q: The density of pure water at 4 °C is about:
questions.x: Water reaches its maximum density, about 1.00 g cm⁻³, at 4 °C. The value 0.92 g cm⁻³ belongs to ice.

questions.q: In most ionic crystals the radius ratio (cation radius / anion radius) is less than 1. This is because:
o: Cations are usually larger than anions
Anions are usually larger than cations
Cations always carry a larger charge
Anions always carry a smaller charge
questions.x: A cation loses electrons and shrinks, while an anion gains electrons and expands, so the cation is usually the smaller ion.

questions.q: In the Born–Haber cycle for sodium chloride, which step (other than forming the lattice) releases energy?
questions.x: Electron gain by a chlorine atom (first electron affinity) is exothermic. Sublimation, bond dissociation and ionisation all absorb energy.

questions.q: The Ksp expression for aluminium hydroxide, Al(OH)₃, is:
questions.x: Al(OH)₃ ⇌ Al³⁺ + 3OH⁻, so Ksp = [Al³⁺][OH⁻]³. The coefficient becomes a power.

questions.q: At 25 °C, Ksp of AgCl is 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰. A solution has [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] = 1 × 10⁻¹². This solution is:
o: Already holding the maximum dissolved AgCl
questions.x: The ionic product 1 × 10⁻¹² is less than Ksp 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰, so the solution is unsaturated and more AgCl could dissolve.

questions.q: The step 2NO + Br₂ → 2NOBr is a single elementary step. Its rate law is:
questions.x: For an elementary step, the powers equal the numbers of each particle colliding: two NO and one Br₂.

questions.q: The exponential term of the Arrhenius expression, which contains Ea, R and T, is a measure of:
o: The total number of collisions per second
The enthalpy change of the reaction
The fraction of molecules that are products at equilibrium
The fraction of collisions with energy equal to or greater than Ea
questions.x: e^(−Ea/RT) is the fraction of collisions energetic enough to react; A relates to collision frequency and orientation.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a reaction intermediate from an activated complex?
o: An intermediate lies at the highest point of the energy profile
An activated complex can be isolated and stored like an intermediate
An intermediate appears in the overall balanced equation
An intermediate lies in an energy dip between steps, while an activated complex exists only at an energy peak
questions.x: An intermediate is formed in one step and used in a later step, sitting in a minimum between two peaks. The activated complex is the fleeting arrangement at the top of a barrier.

questions.q: Which of the following is a spontaneous chemical reaction?
o: Decomposition of water into H₂ and O₂ at room temperature
Rusting of iron in moist air
Conversion of CO₂ and H₂O into glucose in the dark
questions.x: Iron rusts by itself, though slowly. Splitting water or NaCl needs electrical energy, and photosynthesis needs light energy.

questions.q: Which equation represents the standard enthalpy of combustion of carbon monoxide?
questions.x: Enthalpy of combustion is for 1 mol of the substance burning completely. The second equation burns 2 mol, and the last two burn carbon, not CO.

questions.q: Taking w as the work done on the system, the first law of thermodynamics is written as:
questions.x: The change in internal energy equals the heat absorbed plus the work done on the system. With w as work done by the system, it becomes ΔE = q − w.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of chromium in chromium(III) sulphate, Cr₂(SO₄)₃?
questions.x: Three SO₄²⁻ groups give −6, so the two Cr atoms together are +6, i.e. +3 each, as the name shows.

questions.q: In PF₅, phosphorus has five bond pairs and no lone pair. The shape of the molecule is:
questions.x: Five bond pairs give a trigonal bipyramid: three equatorial bonds at 120° and two axial bonds at 90° to them. Six bond pairs would give an octahedron.

questions.q: Grease stains on cloth are removed with petrol rather than with water because:
o: Grease is non-polar and dissolves in non-polar petrol
Grease is ionic and dissolves only in petrol
Water is non-polar and cannot dissolve grease
Petrol reacts chemically with grease to form salts
questions.x: Grease and petrol are both non-polar hydrocarbons, so grease dissolves in petrol. Water is polar and does not dissolve non-polar grease.

questions.q: How many sp³-hybridised carbon atoms are present in pent-1-ene, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₂CH₃?
questions.x: The two carbons of the C=C bond are sp². The remaining three carbons (CH₂, CH₂ and CH₃) form only single bonds, so they are sp³.

questions.q: The element with atomic number 15 is placed in:
questions.x: Z = 15 is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³ (phosphorus): the last electron enters 3p, n = 3 gives period 3, and five outer electrons give Group VA.

questions.q: A small piece of sodium dropped into water floats and melts into a silvery ball. This shows that sodium has:
o: A low density and a low melting point, and the reaction is exothermic
A high density and a high melting point
A low density, and the reaction absorbs heat
A high melting point, and the reaction is slow
questions.x: Sodium is less dense than water, so it floats; the heat released by the reaction is enough to melt it because its melting point is low (about 98 °C).

questions.q: Which two elements of the first transition series have only one electron in the 4s orbital of their ground-state atoms?
questions.x: Cr is 3d⁵ 4s¹ and Cu is 3d¹⁰ 4s¹, because a half-filled or completely filled 3d subshell gives extra stability. The other elements listed have 4s².

questions.q: Which pair of compounds belong to the same class, having the same functional group?
questions.x: Ethanol and propan-1-ol are both alcohols. The other pairs are alcohol and ether, aldehyde and ketone, and carboxylic acid and ester.

questions.q: Most organic compounds dissolve more readily in:
o: Water than in any organic solvent
Molten salts than in organic solvents
Non-polar organic solvents such as benzene or ether than in water
questions.x: Organic compounds are mostly covalent and non-polar or weakly polar, so 'like dissolves like': they dissolve in organic solvents. Some small polar ones, such as ethanol, also dissolve in water.

questions.q: An alkene with a branch next to its CH₂= end, CH₂=CHCH(CH₃)CH₃, is given which systematic name?
questions.x: The chain is numbered from the end nearer the double bond, so C=C is at carbon 1 and the methyl group at carbon 3: 3-methylbut-1-ene.

questions.q: Which reagent distinguishes ethene from ethane at room temperature?
questions.x: Ethene adds bromine and decolourises orange bromine water quickly; ethane, a saturated alkane, does not react in the dark.

questions.q: The colours of the precipitates that ethyne gives with ammoniacal silver nitrate and with ammoniacal copper(I) chloride are, respectively:
questions.x: Silver acetylide, Ag₂C₂, is a white precipitate; copper(I) acetylide, Cu₂C₂, is red (reddish-brown). Both tests show an acidic terminal hydrogen.

questions.q: 0.2 mol of benzene adds chlorine completely in sunlight. What volume of chlorine at STP is used?
questions.x: C₆H₆ + 3Cl₂ → C₆H₆Cl₆, so 0.2 mol benzene needs 0.6 mol Cl₂; 0.6 × 22.4 = 13.44 dm³. 4.48 dm³ ignores the 1 : 3 ratio.

questions.q: 7.8 g of benzene is converted completely into benzene hexachloride, C₆H₆Cl₆ (M = 291 g mol⁻¹). What mass of product is formed? (C 12, H 1)
questions.x: Moles of benzene = 7.8/78 = 0.1. One mole of benzene gives one mole of C₆H₆Cl₆, so mass = 0.1 × 291 = 29.1 g.

questions.q: Propene, CH₃CH=CH₂, is treated with ozone and the ozonide is broken down with zinc and water. The products are:
questions.x: Ozonolysis splits the C=C bond and each carbon becomes C=O: CH₃CH= gives CH₃CHO (ethanal) and =CH₂ gives HCHO (methanal).

questions.q: When an electrophile E⁺ bonds to the benzene ring, the electrons used to form the new C–E bond come from:
o: A C–H bond of the ring
A lone pair on the electrophile
The π electron cloud of the ring
questions.x: The benzene ring acts as an electron-pair donor: two of its π electrons form the new σ bond to E⁺, giving the arenium ion.

questions.q: In the reaction CH₃CH₂I + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂OH + I⁻, the nucleophile and the leaving group are:
o: I⁻ is the nucleophile and OH⁻ is the leaving group
CH₃CH₂I is the nucleophile and OH⁻ is the leaving group
OH⁻ is the nucleophile and I⁻ is the leaving group
CH₃CH₂OH is the nucleophile and I⁻ is the leaving group
questions.x: OH⁻ donates an electron pair to the carbon bonded to iodine, and iodine leaves as I⁻. The alkyl halide is the substrate, not the nucleophile.

questions.q: Ethanol, C₂H₅OH, and methoxymethane, CH₃OCH₃, have the same molecular formula, but ethanol has a much higher boiling point. This is because:
o: Ethanol has an O–H bond, so its molecules hydrogen-bond to one another
Methoxymethane has a larger molar mass
Methoxymethane molecules form stronger hydrogen bonds
questions.x: The two are functional isomers with equal molar masses. Only ethanol has a hydrogen on oxygen, so only ethanol molecules hydrogen-bond to each other; the ether has only weaker dipole forces.

questions.q: Which of the isomeric butyl alcohols (C₄H₉OH) has the lowest boiling point?
questions.x: All four form hydrogen bonds, but branching makes the molecule more compact, reducing surface contact and van der Waals forces. The most branched isomer, 2-methylpropan-2-ol, boils lowest; the straight-chain butan-1-ol boils highest.

questions.q: Which compound does NOT undergo aldol condensation with dilute alkali?
questions.x: Aldol condensation needs a hydrogen on the α-carbon (next to C=O), which the base removes to make a carbanion. Methanal, HCHO, has no α-carbon at all; the other three have α-hydrogens.

questions.q: Propanone reacts with hydroxylamine, NH₂OH, in weakly acidic solution. The organic product is:
questions.x: NH₂OH adds to the C=O and then water is lost (addition–elimination), giving propanone oxime, (CH₃)₂C=NOH. Hydrazine, not hydroxylamine, gives a hydrazone.

questions.q: Reducing the aromatic aldehyde C₆H₅CHO with lithium aluminium hydride gives:
questions.x: The –CHO group becomes –CH₂OH, so the product is benzyl alcohol (phenylmethanol). Benzoic acid would be the oxidation product, not the reduction product.

questions.q: Ethanoic anhydride can be made by heating ethanoic acid with phosphorus pentoxide, P₂O₅. The role of P₂O₅ is to act as a:
o: Dehydrating agent, removing a water molecule from two acid molecules
questions.x: 2CH₃COOH → (CH₃CO)₂O + H₂O; P₂O₅ removes the water, joining two acid molecules into the anhydride.

questions.q: During blood clotting, the soluble plasma protein that is converted into insoluble threads is:
questions.x: Fibrinogen is converted into insoluble fibrin threads, which trap blood cells to form a clot. Albumin stays in solution in the plasma.

questions.q: Azo dyes are prepared by coupling a diazonium salt with:
o: A phenol or an aromatic amine
questions.x: An aryl diazonium ion reacts with an activated aromatic ring such as a phenol or an aromatic amine, joining the two rings through –N=N–. Alkanes and alkyl halides do not couple this way.

questions.q: Vector P has rectangular components Px and Py. The magnitude of vector P is:
questions.x: The two rectangular components are at right angles, so by Pythagoras the magnitude is √(Px² + Py²). Simply adding the components ignores the right angle between them.

questions.q: From a cliff 45 m high a stone is launched horizontally. How many seconds pass before it lands? (g = 10 m s⁻², air drag negligible)
questions.x: Vertically the stone starts with zero velocity and accelerates at g: 45 = ½ × 10 × t², so t² = 9 and t = 3 s, whatever its horizontal speed.

questions.q: A displacement–time graph can never be a vertical straight line, because that would mean the body has:
questions.x: A vertical line would mean a change of position in zero time, i.e. an infinite slope and so an infinite velocity, which is impossible.

questions.q: In the absence of air resistance, the total mechanical energy (kinetic + potential) of a projectile during its flight:
o: Becomes zero at the highest point
questions.x: Without air resistance, only gravity does work on the projectile, so kinetic energy and potential energy change into each other while their sum stays constant.

questions.q: A horse pulls a cart and the cart pulls back on the horse with an equal force. The horse still moves forward because:
o: The horse's pull on the cart is larger than the cart's pull on the horse
Action and reaction forces cancel each other
The ground pushes the horse forward with a force larger than the cart's backward pull on it
The cart's pull acts only after the horse moves
questions.x: Action and reaction act on different bodies. The forces on the horse are the cart's backward pull and the ground's forward push; the horse accelerates when the ground's push is larger.

questions.q: When a bomb initially at rest explodes, the kinetic energy of its fragments comes from:
o: The momentum of the bomb before the explosion
The gravitational pull of the Earth
The chemical energy stored in the explosive
Nothing, because kinetic energy is conserved
questions.x: The bomb starts with zero momentum and zero kinetic energy. The chemical energy of the explosive is changed into kinetic energy, while the total momentum stays zero.

questions.q: A body at rest explodes into exactly two fragments. Just after the explosion the two fragments must move:
o: At right angles to each other
With equal speeds whatever their masses
In opposite directions along the same line
questions.x: Total momentum must stay zero, so the two momenta must be equal and opposite. That needs the fragments to move in exactly opposite directions; their speeds are equal only if their masses are.

questions.q: A hoist with an efficiency of 50% raises a 20 kg crate 5 m in 4 s at constant speed. What electrical power must be supplied to it? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.x: Useful power = mgh/t = 20 × 10 × 5 ÷ 4 = 250 W. Input power = 250 ÷ 0.5 = 500 W. 125 W wrongly multiplies by the efficiency instead of dividing.

questions.q: Two students use different reference levels to work out the gravitational potential energy of the same falling ball. Which quantity will they both find the same?
o: The potential energy of the ball at its starting point
The sign of the potential energy at the floor
The work done by gravity as the ball falls between two given points
The potential energy of the ball at the floor
questions.x: The value and sign of PE at a point depend on the reference level, but the work done by gravity (the change in PE) between two points does not.

questions.q: A sledge comes down a rough snowy hillside without speeding up. Where does the gravitational potential energy it loses go?
o: All of it is dissipated as heat through work done against friction
All of it becomes kinetic energy of the sledge
It is stored as elastic energy in the snow
It becomes extra potential energy at the bottom
questions.x: At constant speed the kinetic energy does not change, so all the gravitational PE lost is used up as work against friction and appears as heat.

questions.q: Which statement about units of angle is correct?
o: One revolution is equal to π rad
The degree is the SI unit of angle
One degree is 1/360 of a revolution
questions.x: The degree is defined as 1/360 of a full revolution. π rad (not 1 rad) equals 180°, a revolution is 2π rad, and the SI unit of angle is the radian.

questions.q: Why can't fixed, smooth streamlines be drawn for turbulent flow?
o: The paths of fluid particles keep changing irregularly and crossing one another
questions.x: In turbulent flow the motion is irregular, with eddies, so particle paths change with time and cross. Streamlines describe only steady (laminar) flow.

questions.q: The pressure in the narrow throat of a Venturi meter is lower than in its wide section because:
o: The fluid moves faster in the throat (continuity), so its pressure falls (Bernoulli)
The fluid moves slower in the throat, so its pressure falls
The fluid's density is lower in the throat
The throat is at a greater height
questions.x: Continuity makes the speed higher where the area is smaller; Bernoulli's effect then gives a lower pressure where the speed is higher.

questions.q: A skydiver is falling straight down at her terminal velocity. During this part of the fall, her kinetic energy:
questions.x: At terminal velocity her speed is constant, so her kinetic energy ½mv² does not change. The gravitational potential energy she loses goes into work against air drag.

questions.q: A siren emits a note of fixed frequency 1000 Hz. As the air warms from 0 °C to 30 °C, the wavelength of the sound in the air:
o: Decreases, because the speed rises while the frequency stays the same
Stays the same, because the frequency is fixed
Decreases, because warm air is less dense
Increases, because the speed rises while the frequency stays the same
questions.x: The speed of sound rises with temperature, while the frequency is fixed by the siren. So λ = v/f increases.

questions.q: In a stationary wave, all particles between two adjacent nodes vibrate:
o: In phase with one another, but with different amplitudes
In phase with one another, with the same amplitude
Out of phase with one another, with the same amplitude
With phases that change steadily from particle to particle
questions.x: Within one loop all particles move up together and down together, but the amplitude varies from zero at the nodes to a maximum at the antinode. A steadily changing phase is a feature of progressive waves.

questions.q: A stretched string has a fundamental frequency of 100 Hz. Its vibrating length is halved and its tension is made 4 times as large. Its new fundamental frequency is:
questions.x: f ∝ √T / L. Halving L doubles f, and 4 times the tension doubles it again: 100 × 2 × 2 = 400 Hz.

questions.q: A wave of amplitude 7 mm and a coherent wave of amplitude 3 mm overlap so that a crest of one always falls on a trough of the other. The amplitude of the resulting vibration is:
questions.x: Crest on trough means opposite phase, so the displacements subtract: 7 − 3 = 4 mm. Complete cancellation would need equal amplitudes.

questions.q: A boat bobs up and down 15 times per minute on sea waves whose crests are 8 m apart. The speed of the waves is:
questions.x: f = 15/60 = 0.25 Hz, so v = fλ = 0.25 × 8 = 2 m s⁻¹. Forgetting to change minutes to seconds gives 120.

questions.q: Electromagnetic waves are produced by:
o: Vibrating particles of a material medium
Charges at rest in a strong field
questions.x: An oscillating, and so accelerating, charge produces changing electric and magnetic fields that travel out as an electromagnetic wave. Charges at rest or in uniform motion do not radiate.

questions.q: A dolphin's click has a wavelength of 1.5 cm in sea water, where sound travels at 1500 m s⁻¹. The frequency of the click is:
questions.x: f = v/λ = 1500/0.015 = 1 × 10⁵ Hz (ultrasound). Forgetting to change 1.5 cm into 0.015 m gives 1000 Hz.

questions.q: A gas behaves ideally and has a molar heat capacity of 33.2 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ when heated at constant pressure. What is its molar heat capacity at constant volume? (R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
questions.x: Cv = Cp − R = 33.2 − 8.3 = 24.9 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Adding R instead of subtracting gives 41.5, and dividing gives 4.0.

questions.q: The SI unit in which a quantity of heat is measured is the:
questions.x: Heat is energy in transfer, so its SI unit is the joule. The kelvin measures temperature, the watt measures power, and the calorie is an older non-SI unit.

questions.q: A proton (charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 500 V. The kinetic energy it gains is:
questions.x: The work done by the field is qV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 500 = 8 × 10⁻¹⁷ J, all of which becomes kinetic energy.

questions.q: An RC circuit has a time constant of 4 s. If the resistance is 2 MΩ, the capacitance is:
For which pair of equal-magnitude point charges do field lines run continuously from one charge to the other?
o: One positive charge and one negative charge
questions.x: Lines start on positive charges and end on negative charges, so they can link the two charges only when the signs are opposite. Like charges give a neutral point between them.

questions.q: Two identical cells, each of emf E and internal resistance r, are connected in series (positive to negative). The combination has:
o: Emf E and internal resistance r/2
questions.x: In series the emfs add and the internal resistances also add, giving 2E and 2r. Parallel identical cells would give E and r/2.

questions.q: The resistivity ρ of the material of a wire of resistance R, length L and cross-sectional area A is given by:
questions.x: From R = ρL/A, rearranging gives ρ = RA/L, which is why the unit of resistivity is Ω m.

questions.q: A charged particle moves in a circle at right angles to a uniform magnetic field. As it goes round, its kinetic energy:
questions.x: The magnetic force is perpendicular to the motion, so it does no work and the speed, hence kinetic energy, does not change.

questions.q: A magnet is moved into a coil in the same way twice, once with 100 turns and once with 300 turns of the same size. Compared with the first coil, the emf in the second coil is:
questions.x: The emf is N times the rate of change of flux per turn. With the same flux change and time, tripling N triples the emf.

questions.q: An ideal transformer takes 0.2 A from a 240 V supply and gives an output of 12 V. The secondary current is:
questions.x: For an ideal transformer, VpIp = VsIs: 240 × 0.2 = 48 W, so Is = 48/12 = 4 A.

questions.q: In a pure capacitor connected to AC, the current leads the voltage because:
o: The capacitor produces a back emf
Charge must flow onto the plates before the voltage across them can build up
The capacitor has very high resistance
The dielectric slows down the electrons
questions.x: The voltage across a capacitor is V = Q/C, so it rises only after charge has flowed. The current is therefore a quarter-cycle ahead.

questions.q: A 4.7 V battery, a 1 kΩ resistor and a silicon diode are connected in series, with the n-side of the diode joined to the positive terminal of the battery. The current is approximately:
questions.x: With the n-side at the positive terminal the diode is reverse biased, so only a negligible current flows. 4 mA would be the answer if it were forward biased: (4.7 − 0.7)/1000.

questions.q: Two photons have energies in the ratio 1 : 4. The ratio of their wavelengths is:
questions.x: E = hc/λ, so wavelength is inversely proportional to energy. Energies 1 : 4 give wavelengths 4 : 1.

questions.q: According to Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom, an electron moving in one of the allowed orbits:
o: Emits a photon on every revolution
questions.x: Bohr postulated stationary orbits in which the electron does not radiate. It emits or absorbs energy only when it jumps between orbits.

questions.q: A neutral atom of aluminium, ²⁷₁₃Al, has how many nucleons and how many electrons?
questions.x: Nucleons = A = 27. A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons, Z = 13.

questions.q: The town museum is open from ten in the morning to five in the evening every day except Monday. Tickets cost 100 rupees for adults and 30 rupees for students who show a college card. Children under five enter free. Visitors may take photographs in the main hall, but not in the coin gallery, where the lights are kept low to protect the old metal. According to the passage, where are photographs NOT allowed?
questions.x: The passage says photographs are allowed in the main hall but not in the coin gallery. The other places are not described as having any ban.

questions.q: In "Whatever you decide will be accepted by the committee", the words 'Whatever you decide' form:
o: A noun clause acting as subject
questions.x: The words have their own subject and verb and act as the subject of 'will be accepted', so they form a noun clause.

questions.q: Choose the correct verb: "At sea level, water ___ at 100 °C."
questions.x: Scientific facts and general truths take the simple present tense.

questions.q: Which word describes a person who is careful with money in a critical, negative way?
questions.x: 'Stingy' suggests meanness about money; 'thrifty', 'economical' and 'prudent' all praise careful spending.

questions.q: In "Her only aim is to pass the exam with distinction", the infinitive phrase 'to pass the exam with distinction' acts as:
questions.x: The subject is 'Her only aim'; the infinitive phrase after the linking verb 'is' completes it as a subject complement.

questions.q: Find the error: "The teacher let us to leave early because of the heat."
questions.x: 'Let' takes the bare infinitive, so it should be 'let us leave'.

questions.q: Change into the passive voice: "Why did the manager dismiss the clerk?"
o: Why did the clerk dismissed by the manager?
Why was the clerk dismissed by the manager?
Why was the clerk dismiss by the manager?
Why the clerk was dismissed by the manager?
questions.x: A simple past question becomes 'Why + was + subject + past participle', keeping question word order.

questions.q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "The job needs patience, skill and being honest."
o: The job needs patience, skill and to be honest.
The job needs patience, skill and honesty.
The job needs being patient, skill and honesty.
The job needs patience, skilful and honesty.
questions.x: Items in a list should have the same grammatical form (parallel structure). 'Patience', 'skill' and 'honesty' are all nouns.

questions.q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "The reason he failed the test is because he did not revise."
o: The reason he failed the test is due to he did not revise.
The reason why he failed the test is because of he did not revise.
The reason he failed the test because he did not revise.
The reason he failed the test is that he did not revise.
questions.x: 'The reason ... is because' repeats the idea of cause; correct usage is 'The reason ... is that ...'. The last version has no main verb for 'the reason', so it is not a complete sentence.

questions.q: No reptile in the zoo has fur. The zoo's python is a reptile. Which statement must be true?
o: The python is the only reptile in the zoo
The zoo's python has no fur
Every animal without fur in the zoo is a reptile
Some mammals in the zoo are reptiles
questions.x: The python belongs to the group 'reptiles in the zoo', and no member of that group has fur. The statements say nothing about which other animals lack fur.

questions.q: Buses will not run on the new road unless it is repaired. Buses are now running on the road. Which statement must be true?
o: Buses run on every repaired road
Cars are not allowed on the road
questions.x: 'Not B unless A' means that if the road is not repaired, buses do not run. Since buses are running, the road must have been repaired.

questions.q: Which number is wrong in the series 3, 12, 48, 190, 768?
questions.x: Each term should be 4 times the one before: 3, 12, 48, 192, 768. So 190 should be 192.

questions.q: Seven people stand in a single queue. Fahad is third from the front. Waleed stands behind Fahad, with exactly two people between them. How many people stand behind Waleed?
questions.x: With two people between them, Waleed is in place 3 + 3 = 6. In a queue of seven, one person stands behind him.

questions.q: A clock gains 2 minutes every hour. It is set to the correct time at 8:00 a.m. Later the same day it shows 2:12 p.m. What is the correct time then?
questions.x: The clock shows 62 minutes for every 60 real minutes. It has shown 6 hours 12 minutes = 372 minutes, which is 372 × 60 / 62 = 360 real minutes, so the time is 2:00 p.m.

questions.q: In a code, PEN is written as ODM. Using the same code, how is INK written?
questions.x: Each letter is moved one place back in the alphabet (P to O, E to D, N to M). So I, N, K become H, M, J.

questions.q: Statement: Many people do not file their income tax returns because the forms are hard to understand. Courses of action: I. The forms should be simplified. II. Help desks and online guides should be provided to assist people. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: Simpler forms remove the difficulty, and help desks support those who still struggle. Both actions follow from the stated cause.

questions.q: Statement: Should hospitals hold free health-check camps in villages? Argument I: Yes, they help find diseases early when treatment is easier. Argument II: No, villagers can travel to cities whenever they wish. Which argument is strong?
o: Both arguments I and II are strong
Neither argument I nor II is strong
questions.x: Early detection is a real and important benefit. Argument II is weak because many villagers cannot easily travel to cities for check-ups.

questions.q: Statement I: An oil tanker ship leaked oil near the coast. Statement II: Many sea birds near the coast were found covered in oil. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
questions.x: The leaked oil spread over the water and coated the birds. The leak came first and caused the harm.
